evidence.quote: the 127-mile Seward Highway holds triple designation: USDA Forest Service Scenic Byway, Alaska Scenic Byway, and All-American Road.

evidence.claim: Building the connection took decades. A road from Seward to Kenai Lake was finished in 1923, followed by the Moose Pass–Hope section in 1937.
evidence.quote: An 18-mile-long (29 km) stretch of the Seward Highway, traveling from Seward to Kenai Lake was completed in 1923. Another segment of the highway, running between Moose Pass and Hope, was completed in 1937.

evidence.claim: The Mile 18 bridge joined the Seward and Moose Pass sections in 1946; the full highway finally connected Seward to Anchorage in 1951.
evidence.quote: The Mile 18 bridge, nicknamed "The Missing Link", which would connect the Seward and Moose Pass portions, was not completed until 1946

evidence.claim: the full highway finally connected Seward to Anchorage in 1951
evidence.quote: The roadway was completed on October 19, 1951, connecting Seward to the major city of Anchorage by road for the first time
The roadway was completed on October 19, 1951

evidence.claim: Paving followed in 1952.
evidence.quote: The entire length of the highway was paved in 1952.

evidence.claim: Then the 1964 earthquake lowered parts of the road below Turnagain Arm’s high-water mark. Crews raised and rebuilt the highway and bridges in 1964–66.
evidence.quote: During the 1964 Alaska earthquake, about 20 miles (32 km) of the Seward Highway sank below the high water mark of Turnagain Arm; the highway and its bridges were raised and rebuilt in 1964–66.

evidence.quote: The route continues through the mountains for about 24 miles (39 km) more, before a steep decline, at which point the highway exits the Kenai Peninsula and continues along the shores Turnagain Arm.
